test_title: PYST 20: Selection Post (Higher Secondary Level) - GA (Held On 02 Aug, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: The Rigveda points to an organized society. What kind of marriage existed there?

options.text: Both monogamy and polygamy was practiced equally
Monogamy was general rule but some princes practiced polygamy

solution:
The correct answer is __**Monogamy was general rule but some princes practiced polygamy**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Rigveda**, which is the oldest of the four **Vedas**, provides a glimpse into the social structure of the **Early Vedic Period** (circa **1500 BCE to 1000 BCE**). In this society, **Monogamy** (the practice of having one spouse at a time) was the established general rule for the vast majority of the population. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• While **Monogamy** was the social norm, **Polygamy** (the practice of having more than one wife) was prevalent among the ruling classes, such as **Princes**, **Kings**, and noble **Kshatriyas**. This was often done for political alliances or to ensure multiple heirs. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.***

• The idea that only **Polygamy** was practiced is historically inaccurate, as the **Rigvedic** hymns frequently celebrate the union of a single husband and wife as a sacred and stable unit of the **Kula** (family). ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Monogamy** and **Polygamy** were not practiced equally; **Monogamy** was the standard for the common **Aryans** (Vis), whereas **Polygamy** was an exception reserved for the elite. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• The **Rigvedic** society was **Patriarchal**, meaning the head of the family was the **Kulapa** (usually the father), but women enjoyed a high status and participated in religious sacrifices alongside their husbands.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Status of Women:** Women in the **Rigvedic** period were not secluded. They received education and some even composed hymns, known as **Brahmavadinis**. Famous examples include **Lopamudra**, **Ghosha**, **Viswavara**, and **Apala**.

• **Marriage Customs:** **Child marriage** was virtually non-existent during this era. Girls were usually married at a mature age, typically between **16 and 17 years**. The **Rigveda** mentions the **Vahatu**, which were gifts given to the bride by her parents, often considered a precursor to the **Dowry** system.

• **Widow Remarriage:** The practice of **Niyoga** (levirate marriage) existed, where a childless widow could marry her **Devar** (younger brother-in-law) to produce a son for the deceased husband's lineage. This indicates a pragmatic approach to family continuity.

• **Types of Union:** While formal marriages were the norm, the **Rigveda** also alludes to **Gandharva Vivaha** (love marriage) and mentions the **Svayamvara** (where a woman chooses her husband), though these became more structured in the **Later Vedic Period**.

• **Social Units:** The basic unit of society was the **Kula** (family). Multiple families formed a **Grama** (village), led by a **Gramani**. A group of villages formed a **Vis** (clan), and the highest political unit was the **Jana** (tribe), headed by a **Rajan** (King).

**Important Points__**

• **Geographical Location:** The **Rigvedic** people lived in the **Saptasindhu** region, which refers to the land of the seven rivers, including the **Indus** (Sindhu), **Vitasta** (Jhelum), **Asikni** (Chenab), **Parushni** (Ravi), **Vipas** (Beas), **Sutudri** (Sutlej), and the **Saraswati**.

• **Religious Significance:** Marriage was viewed as a **Sacrament** rather than a contract. The **Surya-Savitri** hymn in the **10th Mandala** of the **Rigveda** provides the earliest description of wedding rituals, many of which are still followed in **Hindu** weddings today.

• **Polyandry:** There is very little evidence of **Polyandry** (one wife, multiple husbands) in the **Rigveda**, although some scholars point to the mythological story of the **Maruts** and **Rodasi** or the **Ashvins** marrying **Surya** as rare allegorical exceptions.

• **Economic Life:** The **Rigvedic** society was primarily **Pastoral**. **Cattle** (Gau) was the most valued possession and often served as a medium of exchange. The term for a daughter, **Duhitri**, literally means 'one who milks the cow'.
